chunks: Bakr ibn Muhammad narrated from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام:
that a questioner asked him about the time of Maghrib, so he said:
Indeed Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says in His Book concerning Ibrāhīm عليه السلام:
“So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said: This is my Lord.”

So this is the beginning of the time, and the end of that is the disappearance of the twilight. Then the beginning of the time of the later ʿIshāʾ is the going away of the redness, and the end of its time is until the darkening of the night, meaning the middle of the night.

key_terms.ذَهَابُ الْحُمْرَةِ: the fading of the redness in the sky
key_terms.غَسَقِ اللَّيْلِ: the deep darkening of the night
key_terms.غَيْبُوبَةُ الشَّفَقِ: the disappearance of twilight marking the end of Maghrib time
key_terms.وَقْتِ الْمَغْرِبِ: the prescribed time of the Maghrib prayer

ai.seo_question: When do the times of Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ begin and end in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the legal timing of the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers. It indicates that Maghrib begins with the onset of night and ends with the disappearance of the twilight, while ʿIshāʾ begins with the fading of the redness and continues until midnight.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.657 - Bakar ibn Muhammad narrated from Imam Jafar ibn Muhammad Al-Sadiq (as) that a person asked him about the timing of Maghrib.

Imam (as) said: "Indeed, Allah (swt), Blessed and Exalted, mentions in His Book concerning Ibrahim (as), 'When the night covered him, he saw a star and said: "This is my Lord (azj)."'
This marks the beginning of the Maghrib time.
The end of this time is the disappearance of twilight (Shafaq). The start of the Isha prayer is marked by the fading of the redness (twilight), and its end extends until the middle of the night”.
